title: TCP and UDP
lead: Connection setup, ordering, and acknowledgments versus speed and simplicity — and why a given application ends up choosing one protocol over the other.

sections.title: One question: does it need a guarantee

blocks.text: Both protocols run at the fourth layer, and both carry **ports** to separate applications on the same host. From there, they diverge.

head: TCP
UDP
rows: voice, video, DNS, DHCP, SNMP, TFTP

blocks.title: Remember
paras: UDP isn't chosen because "delivery doesn't matter" — it's chosen because **retransmission is useless**: a voice packet that arrives 300 ms late is worthless anyway, and resending it would only add delay.

blocks.text: Teardown is four steps (FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK), or an abrupt reset with a single **RST**.
This gets tested as "which flag do you see first," "how many messages does setup take," and "what does RST in a capture mean" (the connection was refused or reset, the port is closed).

sections.title: What the TCP header fields do

items: **Sequence number** — the number of the first byte in the segment: the receiver uses it to reassemble the stream in the right order.
**Acknowledgment number** — the number of the next byte expected, i.e., "everything up to this has been received."

**Window size** — how many bytes the sender may send without an acknowledgment. This is **flow control**: the receiver shrinks the window when it can't keep up with its buffer, and grows it when it can. A zero-size window means "wait, I'm overwhelmed."
**Flags** — SYN, ACK, FIN, RST, PSH, URG.

blocks.text: The UDP header has only four fields: source port, destination port, length, checksum. No sequence numbers, no window — which is why it's 8 bytes.

head: Port
Protocol
Transport
rows: UDP (TCP for zone transfers and large responses)

blocks.text: Ranges: **0–1023** — well-known, **1024–49151** — registered, **49152–65535** — dynamic (the client picks one of these as its source port; NAT/PAT uses it to tell sessions apart).

sections.title: Walking through a problem: reading a list of active sessions

blocks.text: An engineer is given this output and asked what's going on:
What to read here, in order:

items: **The first two lines** — two separate TCP connections to the same server on port 443 (HTTPS), distinguished only by the source port. That's two browser tabs to the same site, not an error or a duplicate.

**The third line** — the local SSH service is **listening** for incoming connections (`LISTENING`), but no session has been established yet — foreign address `0.0.0.0:0` means "nobody has connected yet."

**The UDP lines** — UDP has no `ESTABLISHED`/`LISTENING` state at all, so the State column is usually a dash or a loose "active": 68 is the DHCP client, 5353 is mDNS (device discovery on the local segment).

blocks.text: The takeaway the exam is after: the **State** column is only meaningful for TCP; for UDP, its absence isn't a sign of a problem — it's a property of the protocol.

blocks.title: Trap
paras: DNS runs **over both UDP and TCP**: an ordinary query is UDP/53; a zone transfer, or a reply too big to fit, is TCP/53. The "UDP only" answer to a DNS question isn't always correct — read carefully what's actually being asked.

sections.title: Sockets and how sessions are told apart

blocks.text: A session is uniquely identified by a five-tuple: **protocol + source IP + source port + destination IP + destination port**. That's why two browser windows to the same site don't get confused — they have different dynamic source ports.

sections.title: Why an application chose this particular protocol

items: **Voice and video (RTP)** — UDP: consistent latency matters, and a lost packet is easier to mask than to wait for a retransmission.
**DHCP** — UDP: the client doesn't have an address yet, so there's nothing to establish a connection with or from; messages are broadcast.
**TFTP** — UDP: the protocol is deliberately simple and implements all its reliability itself, which is why it fits into a device's bootloader.
**Web, mail, file transfer** — TCP: a single lost byte can render a file unusable.
**SNMP** — UDP: polling hundreds of devices shouldn't cost a connection for each one.

sections.title: Walking through data transfer step by step: seq and ack in motion

blocks.text: The handshake above shows the start, but questions often ask you to trace the numbers **further**, into the data transfer itself. After the connection is established (SYN=x, SYN-ACK=y), the client sends a 500-byte request.

The rule being tested here: **the acknowledgment number equals the sequence number of the byte the sender expects next**, i.e., the received segment's sequence number plus its length in bytes (SYN and FIN each count as one byte, which is why seq=x+1 follows SYN=x). A server that sent 2000 bytes of reply starting at seq=y+1 receives `ack=y+2001` from the client — not "an ack for every packet separately," but a single ack covering the entire contiguous block of data received so far (this is called **cumulative acknowledgment**).

sections.title: Diagnostic: browser "hangs," and the capture shows only SYN with no reply

blocks.text: **Symptom.** A user opens a website, the tab spins, and after a minute it shows a timeout. A `ping` to the server succeeds.
**What to check.** A packet capture from the client:

12:00:01.001  Client → Server  [SYN]  seq=0
12:00:04.001  Client → Server  [SYN]  seq=0   (retransmission)
12:00:10.001  Client → Server  [SYN]  seq=0   (retransmission)
12:00:22.001  Client → Server  [SYN]  seq=0   (retransmission)

**What it means.** The client is faithfully retransmitting SYN with an exponentially growing interval (normal TCP stack behavior on packet loss or no response) — and never receives either a SYN-ACK or an RST. Since `ping` (ICMP, L3) reaches the host but the TCP segment doesn't reach the port, the cause isn't the route — it's that specific port: an ACL or a stateful firewall somewhere on the path is **silently dropping** SYN to that TCP port, without responding at all. This differs from the next scenario.
Two different messages for the same underlying unreachability — and they mean different things:

head: Message
What happened on the wire
Where to look
rows: an `RST` came back in response to the `SYN`
the host is reachable, the port is closed — the service isn't running or isn't listening on that port
no response at all, the client only retransmits `SYN`
the packet was silently dropped — an ACL/firewall on the path, or the host is physically unreachable

blocks.text:
PC> telnet 10.3.3.30 3389
Trying 10.3.3.30...
% Connection refused by remote host

`refused` in this output is direct proof that TCP reached the host; `Trying...` hanging with no response, on the other hand, is a signal to look at filtering along the path rather than at the server itself.

blocks.title: Remember
paras: RST is a response from a live stack that has nothing listening on that port. Silence means either the host is unreachable at L3 (in which case ping fails too), or someone is filtering that specific traffic without notifying the sender.

sections.title: Diagnostic: voice breaks up while web browsing on the same link is fine

blocks.text: **Symptom.** In a parallel IP telephony call, there are clicks and dropped words, while ordinary web browsing and file transfers over the same link don't complain.
**What to check.** Count drops and jitter, not throughput:

R1# show interfaces gi0/1 | include drops|output errors
  Output queue: 0/40 (size/max)
  Total output drops: 128

**What it means.** The interface shows **output drops** — the queue briefly overflows under peak load. TCP web traffic simply won't notice this loss visibly: the sender shrinks its window, resends the lost segment, and the page opens a fraction of a second later. Voice, riding on **RTP over UDP**, has no retransmission — a lost packet is gone for good, and the receiver's jitter buffer either smooths it over (a fraction-of-a-second silence) or doesn't (a click, a dropped word). The practical takeaway tested here is: **TCP hides loss at the cost of delay; UDP exposes loss to the user immediately** — and for voice, that's the lesser evil compared to the delay from retransmission. The actual fix isn't at the transport-layer level, but through QoS queuing with priority for voice traffic — a topic for another chapter.

sections.title: Flow control: working through a window problem

blocks.text: A client with a window size of 4000 bytes and an RTT (round-trip time) of 100 ms can only receive a continuous stream from the server if acknowledgments arrive faster than the window runs out.
Throughput ≈ window / RTT = 4000 bytes / 0.1 s = 40,000 bytes/s ≈ 320 kbit/s

Even if the link itself is capable of a gigabit, **this particular session's** transfer rate is capped at 320 kbit/s until the receiver grows its window (which it does dynamically, as long as it can keep up with its buffer). The exam logic here: a small window on a slow or congested link isn't a malfunction — it's deliberate **flow control**, protecting the receiver from being overwhelmed, not the protocol being stingy.

sections.title: MSS: how much data actually fits in one segment

blocks.text: **Maximum Segment Size** is a field the two sides exchange right in the SYN and SYN-ACK, well before any data transfer, and it's directly tied to the MTU covered in the encapsulation chapter:

Ethernet MTU                 1500 bytes
− IP header (no options)       20 bytes
− TCP header (no options)      20 bytes
= MSS                        1460 bytes

Each side announces its own MSS value (usually derived from its outgoing interface's MTU), and **the smaller of the two announced values is used** — exactly the way the window is limited by the slower side. If there's a tunnel along the path (GRE, IPsec) that adds its own header bytes, the MSS needs to be manually reduced on both ends — otherwise you get the "small packets go through, large packets effectively run into trouble" situation familiar from MTU diagnostics in the previous chapter, just at the transport layer.

sections.title: Diagnostic: file copies slowly, capture shows a lot of Retransmission

blocks.text: **Symptom.** Copying a large file over TCP takes several times longer than expected, even though the link isn't fully loaded.
**What to check.** The retransmission ratio in a traffic capture:

1000 segments sent
   870 acknowledged on the first try
   130 marked as [TCP Retransmission] or [TCP Dup ACK]

**What it means.** A 13% retransmission rate isn't the window (the window controls speed, not loss) and isn't MSS (which just caps the size of each chunk). This much retransmission almost always points to **packet loss along the path** — a congested link, poor Wi-Fi, a misbehaving interface (see the CRC/input error counters from the OSI models chapter). TCP compensates for loss with retransmission, so the transfer doesn't formally break — but each retransmission is a timeout wait cycle, or a **fast retransmit** (three duplicate ACKs in a row force the sender to resend a segment without waiting for the full timer), plus, typically, a shrunken congestion window (**congestion window**) after every such loss. The result is a file that finishes downloading but noticeably slower than the clean link would allow. Exam takeaway: a slow but not-broken TCP transfer points to loss along the path, not a lack of bandwidth as such.

blocks.title: Trap
paras: "Transfer speed is low — the link is narrow" isn't always right: TCP deliberately slows down in response to loss (congestion control), so the real cause of a slow transfer is often loss on an intermediate link, not the bandwidth at either end.

sections.title: Summary: five transport-layer symptoms and where to look

head: Symptom
What to check
Likely cause
rows: Timeout, SYN with no reply, ping succeeds
ACL/firewall on the path to that TCP port
the service on the target port
Voice breaks up, files transfer fine
output drops on interfaces along the path
UDP/RTP lacks priority in the queue
DNS doesn't resolve, no explicit error
arrival of an ICMP port unreachable
service unavailable, or ICMP is filtered

blocks.text: The general logic behind all five rows is the same: first confirm the problem isn't at L3 (`ping`, host reachability), then look at what the transport layer does — or doesn't — report, and only then move to the specific cause. Silence almost always means filtering somewhere along the path, not a failure at the endpoint.

sections.title: TCP connection states: what `show tcp brief` shows

blocks.text: A TCP connection doesn't just live in "established / not established" — it has intermediate states, and those get tested too.

R1# show tcp brief all
TCB       Local Address           Foreign Address        (state)
665F2A18  10.1.1.1.23             10.1.1.10.51223         ESTAB
665F3B20  10.1.1.1.179            10.2.2.2.44012           SYNSENT
665F1C90  10.1.1.1.23             *.*                      LISTEN

head: State
What's happening
rows: the service is up and waiting for an incoming SYN, no connection yet
the local side sent a SYN and is waiting for a SYN-ACK
a SYN arrived, a SYN-ACK was sent, waiting for the final ACK
the handshake is complete, data is flowing
one side has started closing the connection
the connection is closed, but the socket is still held (usually 2 minutes) — in case the final ACK was lost

blocks.text: Practical implication: if `show tcp brief` shows dozens of entries stuck in `SYN_RECEIVED` for weeks, never moving to `ESTABLISHED`, that's the fingerprint of a **SYN flood** — an attacker sends SYNs in bulk and never completes the handshake, filling up the half-open connection table. A single entry stuck in `SYN_SENT` for a long time is the same silently-filtered-response case discussed above. A large number of sessions in `TIME_WAIT` on a busy server usually isn't a problem in itself, but a consequence of short-lived HTTP connections being closed one after another correctly; it only becomes a warning sign when sockets start running out for new connections.

sections.title: Diagnostic: DNS doesn't resolve, but there's no connection error

blocks.text: **Symptom.** An application simply gets no response to a DNS query and, after a while, reports "server not found" — with no explicit "refused" or "unreachable."

**What to check.** The protocol under DNS: UDP, which has no SYN, no RST, and no other explicit "port closed" signal at the transport layer — only the plain fact of no response. The only hint that can come back over the network is ICMP:
ICMP Type 3, Code 3 — Destination Unreachable (Port Unreachable)

**What it means.** If ICMP port unreachable arrives, the server is alive, but the service on UDP/53 isn't listening (not running, or on the wrong port). If nothing arrives at all, either the host is unreachable at L3, or the message is being filtered along the path — much like ICMP Fragmentation Needed in the example from the encapsulation chapter. The key takeaway for the exam: **UDP has no equivalent of RST** — that information is never carried in the protocol body itself, only optionally through ICMP or through the application's own logic (a DNS resolver will simply time out and try the next server on its list).

blocks.title: Trap
paras: "Connection refused" sounds like a TCP-specific term for a reason — UDP has no "refused" in the strict handshake sense, because there's no handshake. A question phrased as "connection refused for a UDP-based service" almost always describes an ICMP port unreachable, not a protocol flag.

items: "Which two characteristics describe UDP?" — connectionless, no acknowledgments, minimal overhead, well suited for voice.
"What is the purpose of the window size field?" — flow control.
"Refer to the exhibit… which protocol is used?" — by the port number in the output.
"Which protocol is used by a client to obtain an IP address automatically?" — DHCP over UDP 67/68.
"Why is UDP preferred for voice?" — low latency, retransmission is useless.
Port-to-protocol matching in drag-and-drop questions.
"A host receives a TCP RST in response to a connection attempt. What does this indicate?" — the host is reachable, but the port is closed or the service isn't listening — not a network problem.

"A client repeatedly retransmits SYN segments and never receives a response. Ping to the same host succeeds. What is the most likely cause?" — an ACL or firewall along the path silently dropping traffic on that specific TCP port.
"Which acknowledgment number will host B send after receiving a 500-byte segment with sequence number 1000?" — 1500: ack = sequence + length of data received.

"Why does TCP handle packet loss differently from UDP in terms of user experience?" — TCP masks the loss through retransmission and delay; UDP hands the loss straight to the application, with no retransmission.

"What is a disadvantage of a very small TCP window size on a high-bandwidth link?" — the session's throughput is capped by the window divided by RTT, which can fall far short of what the link itself can carry.
"What is the purpose of the Maximum Segment Size (MSS)?" — to set the largest chunk of data that fits in one TCP segment, so the resulting packet doesn't exceed the path's MTU.

"A file transfer completes but takes much longer than expected. A capture shows a high percentage of retransmissions. What is the likely cause?" — packet loss along the path (congestion, a misbehaving link), not a lack of bandwidth as such.
"What condition is indicated by many connections stuck in the SYN_RECEIVED state?" — a likely SYN flood: half-open connections that are deliberately never completed.

"Which field changes when a packet passes through a device that adds encapsulation, such as a GRE or IPsec tunnel?" — the effective path MTU shrinks, and MSS on both ends needs to be adjusted manually, or larger segments will be lost or fragmented.

items.q: How many messages does it take to establish a TCP connection, and what are they called?
The receiver sends a window size of 0. What does that mean, and what will the sender do?
items.a: The receiver's buffer is full; the sender will pause transmission until the window is updated.

items.q: An application sends short requests to hundreds of devices and can tolerate a lost reply. Which transport makes sense?
items.a: UDP — this is how, for example, SNMP works.

items.q: Which ports do SSH, Telnet, and HTTPS run on?
What's the difference between the acknowledgment number and the sequence number?
items.a: Sequence is the number of the first byte in this segment; acknowledgment is the number of the next byte expected, confirming everything up to it.

items.q: Telnet to a port returns Connection refused. What does that mean for the network?
items.a: The network is fine: the TCP segment reached the host, but there's no service listening on that port, or it explicitly rejected the connection — an RST came back.

items.q: A client repeatedly retransmits SYN and gets neither a SYN-ACK nor an RST, even though ping to the host succeeds. Where should you look?
items.a: Not at the host itself (it responds to ICMP), but along the path — an ACL or stateful firewall is silently dropping traffic on that TCP port.

items.q: Why aren't voice call dropouts fixed the same way as losses during a file download?
items.a: A file transfer runs over TCP, and a lost segment simply gets re-requested at the cost of a small delay; voice runs over RTP on top of UDP with no retransmission — a lost packet is gone for good, and the fix is QoS priority in the queue, not resending data.

items.q: The receiver's window is 4000 bytes, the link's RTT is 100 ms. What's the maximum throughput of this session, even on a gigabit link?
items.a: About 320 kbit/s (4000 bytes / 0.1 s) — the session is limited by the window, not the physical link speed, until the window grows.

items.q: What makes up an MSS of 1460 bytes with a typical Ethernet MTU of 1500?
items.a: 1500 minus 20 bytes of IP header minus 20 bytes of TCP header (no options) = 1460.

items.q: A DNS query over UDP got no response. What signal on the network could indicate the port is closed, and does the application usually receive it?
items.a: An ICMP Destination Unreachable, Port Unreachable code — but it's optional and often filtered, so the application usually only learns about the problem from its own timeout.

items.q: A capture shows hundreds of connections stuck in the SYN_RECEIVED state, never reaching ESTABLISHED. What does that suggest?
items.a: Likely a SYN flood: an attacker sends SYNs in bulk and deliberately never completes the handshake, filling up the server's half-open connection table.
